data.hypothesis: The selected four-target, 128-thread mapping was correct but measured 0.004165 s, slower than the 0.001844 s baseline; the earlier two-target, 128-thread mapping measured 0.002585 s. Using two targets per thread with 64 threads and 128 targets per block tests whether smaller blocks and greater block-level parallelism improve performance, while still reusing each source load across two targets. The additional block count or reduced lanes per block may instead hurt; no speedup is assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: In this T2 campaign, test block size and target coarsening independently against the baseline; correctness and source reuse do not establish a speedup.
memory_lessons.claim: The recorded two-target and four-target candidates were correct but slower than the baseline. The measurements do not establish the cause.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this two-target, 64-thread mapping across the official scored sizes after full correctness checks.

data.notes: This is a new two-target-per-thread mapping with block=64 and items_per_block=128. Each valid output is written once; partial final groups are guarded independently. The kernel uses no shared memory. The controller must perform correctness checks and official measurements; no result is claimed.
transformations: Set block=64 and items_per_block=128 with shared_memory_bytes=0.
Map each thread to targets blockIdx.x*(2*blockDim.x)+threadIdx.x and that index plus blockDim.x.
Load each source position and mass once per source iteration, then reuse those register values across the two target calculations.
Guard each target independently for partial groups and write each valid output exactly once.
Use no shared-memory source tiling or block-level multi-output assignment.
